headline: Little Island, Big Ideas: How New York’s Most Unusual Outdoor Venue Crafts Its Lineup
summary_text: For the last three seasons, Winokur has served as the producing artistic director of Little Island, the artificial island/public park adjacent to Manhattan's Meatpacking District in the Hudson River which opened five years ago. ... While the Juilliard-educated Winokur had directed, produced and/or cocreated theatrical and opera productions prior to this gig (he also co-founded the imaginative American Modern Opera Company in 2017 and serves as its artistic director), Little Island at Pier 55 is unlike any other performance space in a city that has no shortage of them. Not only is it outdoors, but, as the name suggests, it's a literal island. Unlike, say, theatrical performances in Central Park, Little Island presents artists and innovators with the opportunity to shape the audio-visual experience of an entire discrete outdoor space. ... This season, Little Island features new works from returning musical iconoclasts (Justin Vivian Bond opens the season with Summer's Eve from July 29-31; Anthony Roth Costanzo takes a tour through minimalist music history from Aug. 5-9; Laurie Anderson participates in Thomas Bartlett's Allen Ginsberg at 100 from Sept. 2-6) as well as excavations of New York City's rich musical foundations (The Late Show with Stephen Colbert bandleader Louis Cato brings the music of the Savoy and Harlem Renaissance back to raucous life from Aug. 19-23; three-time Grammy winner Cécile McLorin Salvant explores the edges of Tin Pan Alley from Aug. 12-16). ... Additionally, creative trailblazers are bringing their distinct visions to the island. Tony winner Qween Jean throws a Summer Legacy Ball extravaganza on Aug. 1, and from Aug. 27-30, Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez premiere Marina, "an underwater fairytale about love, belonging and catfishing" (what else would you expect from the boundary-free brain of Torres?) commissioned by the 2026 Whitney Biennial. ... Throughout the entire season, Papi Juice parties — thrown by the Brooklyn DJ/art collective centered around uplifting queer and trans people of color — will bring free dance parties to the island's "Play Ground." The Papi Juice parties always dovetail with one of the performances at The Amph, Little Island's 700-plus-seat amphitheater – meaning you can catch a show, grab a drink and shake your thing all on the same night on the same island. ... Ahead of Little Island's 2026 season, Billboard spoke with Winokur about how he approaches programming the bespoke space, what we can expect from this year's slate and why certain Little Island performances remind him of MTV Unplugged or "the parade of animals going to the Big Apple Circus." ... It actually is a weird, circuitous route. Before the park was built, I was starting my own company, the American Modern Opera Company, AMOC, and we were in conversations to do a show well before the park was built. That never happened. And then when it opened in the first summer, Mikki Shepard ran this really beautiful free festival that was super dense — I think it was just one month, but just gigantic. And my company did a show of all Julius Eastman's music that was the closing night of the opening festival. Then Barry Diller [billionaire businessperson who commissioned Little Island] called me and asked me to think about a new approach to programming, and we came up with this thought of doing more original programming. I started my first season in 2024. ... I think the thing that we were most excited about, and certainly I was most excited about, was a couple of things. One is that we so rarely think of performance as part of public art, and the idea of doing shows in a public park feels incredibly special. So one of the points was to bring a real high-low sensibility to a public space and to make it as accessible as possible, which is why so much of our programming is free and the maximum ticket price is $25. And I was always really interested in extraordinary people, and people particularly who live here or are inflected by the city in one way or another. I think so many of the things that we're doing this year, and that we've reflected on in the past, are about different scenes or icons from the past, the present and the future, all colliding in one place on the island. If that makes sense. ... Yeah, it's just affected life. It's really tough. We do our best to just put on the show, no matter what. There are certain things that we just can't do because it's unsafe — with lightning or whatever. But thankfully, we're at night, so by evening it usually is a tolerable heat. And one of the things I feel like people don't always know is that, in addition to delicious lemonade and water, there are also cocktails available and a liquor license across the entire island, so you can always be drinking, which I think helps mediate any weather issues at all. ... , one of the things I've always loved about this space is that it's a thrust stage, so it's actually really intimate, even though it's over 700 seats. You're never that far away from any performer, and that intimacy is something we've ... I've also always loved the fact that it's wonderful that every show has always been sold out, and that even when things are packed and the standing rail is packed, if you are a tourist or a local who's just walking in the neighborhood and didn't expect to see a show, you still can get one. We've linked all of the speaker systems throughout the park so that the music happening in The Glade or in The Amph can be heard in the Play Ground. You have these beautiful vantage points from all of the pathways, so if you don't have a ticket, you can still see and experience the show in a really fabulous way. I don't think there is another theater that just doesn't have walls. What that symbol means in the city, to me, is one of the greatest gifts that's ever happened. ... I'm a very hands-on producer. Particularly on past commissions, like Figaro or Twyla, it's incredibly involved and hands-on. I think that good creative producing is being a collaborator, not just being an investor. On many of the projects we have this season that are more concert based, it's just an incredibly delicious tossing around of ideas — being a sounding board and a thought partner to everybody. ... Today I did a couple of site visits with designers and lighting designers, to step onto the stage and make sure we've walked through it, looking at what's possible. I have an unbelievable, incredibly dedicated team. Once we go into production, it's this wild thing where we are in the office and then we are at all of the shows, making sure that everything is good. ... I'm there basically every single night, and it's one of the treats. If I'm being totally honest, I've basically lived here since I was 15, and I had never spent a summer in New York until I got this job — like a full summer. To be able to be on the island with all of the visitors, and have a drink, have a snack, and then take in a free show in the Glade, and then a beautiful show in the amphitheater, and then one of these Papi Juice parties — it's amazing. It's just a totally amazing place. ... And back to an earlier question about what I'm learning about the space — one of the things that feels really amazing that we learned, I think with Arthur Russell first, was that we could do six hours of uninterrupted music, and we could also transform how people entered the space. There was this whole drone improvisation with Sam Amidon and Laurie Anderson walking around with their instruments throughout the entire park. ... Those moments where the whole 2.4-acre park becomes one big idea and one canvas is something we're exploring more this year and is something you can't do anywhere else. It would be like a Broadway show getting to control the entire street they're on. The drinks, the food, what you're hearing when you step across the highway onto that bridge — being able to design that entire experience is very special.

summary_text: EXCLUSIVE: Sister Group is entering its “next phase” after turning a profit for the first time in six years. ... Chris Fry, CFO at the Black Doves and The Woman in Cabin 10 producer, told Deadline Sister “refocused on our strengths” in 2025 after shutting down its U.S. hub, and is now looking to the future. The “next phase” will be driven by “delivering best-in-class storytelling from a UK base to a global audience” while potential acquisitions in the vein of docs indie Dorothy Street and digital-first label After Party Studios could be incoming, he added. ... Deadline has seen Sister Group’s financial filing for 2025 and it showed adjusted EBITDA in the black for the first time since the group launched in 2019, rising by around £7M ($9.4M) to £3.8M. Overall profit for the year was £3.3M. Net assets rose sharply to £12.4M. ... Launched in 2019 by Jane Featherstone and Liz Murdoch, Sister Group incorporates the likes of drama indie Sister Pictures, which launched in 2015, New York-based independent publisher Zando, Richard Bacon’s Yes Yes Media and live music venue Koko. Its constituent parts including Sister Pictures have turned a profit in the past but this year is the first time the overall Sister Group hasn’t been in the red. ... Revenue in 2025 did slip, however, by 22% to £56.6M, which the filing said “reflects smaller budgets on the productions completed in 2025, with a larger proportion being sold to public sector broadcasters versus the prior year.” ... Sister has made numerous shows and movies for streamers down the years including the likes of Black Doves and Eric for Netflix, but last year saw well-regarded series for public broadcasters like the BBC’s Waiting for the Out and ITV’s Coldwater starring Andrew Lincoln. These lower-budget shows generate less revenue upfront but Sister holds the IP, which is beneficial further down the road. Revenue in the TV division dipped, according to the filing, while it rose in movies, mainly due to Netflix’s hit The Woman in Cabin 10. Big streamer projects are to come in the shape of Black Doves Season 2 and Apple TV’s Prodigies starring Will Sharpe and Ayo Edebiri. ... Sister’s “next phase” is seeing the rapid continuation of the closure of the U.S. office, which was run by ex-Netflix TV boss Cynthia Holland but shuttered in late 2024 after a review amid tough market conditions. Holland and fellow high-profile execs like Jane Wiseman and Efrain Miron exited. Sister Group’s results revealed that the U.S. wind-down is now “substantially complete” and will be fully done by 2027, with a loss of just £2.5M taken last year compared to £34.5M the prior one. Sister executives have always stressed they will continue to seek work from American buyers and have a footprint there in the shape of Zando and podcast maker Campside Media. ... “We’ve refocused on our strengths – delivering best-in-class storytelling from a UK base to a global audience – and it’s great to see this strategy validated by the numbers,” said Fry. ... The results indicated a number of potential bumps in the road going forwards including “the costs of production having risen to a point whereby UK public sector broadcasters… are funding smaller proportions of budgets” and the “continued shift in consumer viewing habits towards content on social platforms.” “Rapid advancement of AI capabilities combined with uncertainty around audience appetite, legal and ethical guardrails” was also cited. ... Many of Sister’s scripted rivals are now part of the enormous combined Banijay-All3Media operation but there is no suggestion the group is looking for a buyer or to become part of a larger group.

headline: Disney and ABC sue FCC over early license renewals, alleging "a retaliatory campaign" - CBS News
summary_text: Disney and ABC sue FCC over early license renewals, alleging "a retaliatory campaign" - CBS News ... The Walt Disney Company, ABC and their television stations sued the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday, alleging the agency's request to file for early license renewal violates their First Amendment rights and amounts to "a retaliatory campaign." ... The ABC licenses were originally scheduled for renewal between 2028 and 2031. ... The lawsuit, filed in a federal court in Washington, D.C., seeks to halt the FCC's early renewal request and stem the possibility of the agency intervening in or influencing ABC's editorial decisions. The media companies allege that the agency's regulatory actions are intended to punish ABC for "content and viewpoints the Administration dislikes" and threaten all broadcasters, not just ABC. ... "Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts," ABC wrote in the 45-page complaint. ... The lawsuit comes after the agency in April ordered an accelerated review of Disney's ABC-owned television stations, which it said was related to an ongoing investigation into the company's diversity, equity and inclusion practices. The announcement followed President Trump's call for late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel to be fired over a joke he made about first lady Melania Trump. ... Mr. Trump has also previously said ABC should lose its broadcast license over the network's coverage decisions. ... "Disney is obviously very concerned about the FCC's proceeding, as evidenced by their ongoing campaign of disinformation as well as their decision to ask a court to stop the FCC from further pursuing matters," an FCC spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "The FCC will continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead." ... Experts previously told CBS News that the timing of the FCC's order was "highly suspect" and likely related to the president's call to fire Kimmel rather than the FCC's DEI investigation. ... Before its request to ABC, the FCC had not called for an early license renewal in over 50 years, according to Disney and ABC's legal filing. ... The agency has the authority to revoke broadcast licenses, but would face an extremely high legal bar, according to experts. Another course of action would be to decline to renew ABC's licenses, although that would likely lead to a protracted legal battle. ... Disney declined to comment. The company owns eight TV stations, including WABC-TV in New York and KABC-TV in Los Angeles. ... headline: Paramount seeks $1.88B bond from state AGs to cover WBD merger delay costs
summary_text: Paramount seeks $1.88B bond from state AGs to cover WBD merger delay costs ... - Paramount is requesting a judge force the states that filed an antitrust lawsuit against its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery to pay the fees associated with delaying the close of the deal. - A trial between Paramount and the group of state AGs is set for March. - Paramount is requesting a $1.88 billion bond based on its calculation of ticking fees and other costs it will have to pay due to the holdup. ... Paramount Skydance will seek to force the states holding up its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery to pay for the fees and costs associated with the delay, according to a new filing in the antitrust case Monday. ... Paramount is requesting a $1.88 billion bond that would be posted by the states behind the lawsuit. In July, a dozen state attorneys general led by California's Rob Bonta filed to challenge the proposed $110 billion merger between Paramount and WBD. ... The proposed deal would combine two storied film studios — Paramount and Warner Bros. — as well as put together a sprawling portfolio of pay-TV networks in the U.S. and streaming platforms HBO Max and Paramount+. ... The group of state attorneys general said in its initial filing that the merger would violate the Clayton Antitrust Act, which is the more-than- 100-year-old law that prohibits anticompetitive mergers and acquisitions. ... Paramount has received regulatory approvals from the Antitrust Division of the U.S. Department of Justice, as well as all other global jurisdictions needed to move forward with the merger. But last month, Paramount agreed to delay the proposed acquisition to as late as June 2027 while the state AGs' case heads to trial. ... Paramount long planned to have the deal closed by the end of September. The delay could prove costly for Paramount. ... Paramount agreed to a so-called ticking fee under the terms of the merger agreement, meaning that beginning Sept. 30 it would pay WBD shareholders an additional 25 cents per share, per quarter, until the deal closes. The amount could add up to roughly $650 million in cash value per quarter. ... "By the time trial concludes and the parties submit their final briefs, Paramount will have paid Warner Bros. shareholders an unrecoverable $1.3 billion in ticking fees alone," Paramount said in the filing. "Delay also threatens to nullify the regulatory approvals that Defendants have already spent months securing." ... Bonta's office in its statement said, "Paramount and Warner Bros. are two sophisticated companies who willfully decided to include a costly ticking fee as a provision in their merger contract. They knew this merger would undergo regulatory review; they knew it was not a done deal; and they chose to include it anyway.""What's more, Paramount itself stipulated to the timing it is now protesting — they agreed to the dates and did not request a bond as a condition of agreeing not to close until after the trial, and potentially as late as June 2027. Now, they're trying to get a do-over," Bonta's statement said. ... In Paramount's statement, the company said that the $1.88 billion amount is a "straightforward calculation of the maximum potential ticking consideration and financing costs from this litigation." ... However, the statement goes on to add that these are not the only costs associated with delaying the deal: "By virtue of what will be at least an eight-month delay in closing, there will be no integration and no ramped-up investment in content, production, and creative talent by the combined company. Of course, in addition, employees of both Paramount and WBD are also harmed by the uncertainties caused by the delay." ... In addition to California, the group of states suing to block the merger includes Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

headline: SpaceX shows strong growth in its first earnings report since going public - CBS News
summary_text: SpaceX shows strong growth in its first earnings report since going public - CBS News ... SpaceX on Tuesday reported booming revenue and shrinking losses in its first quarterly earnings report as a publicly traded company, offering a window into its performance after executing the biggest ever initial public offering in June. ... NEW YORK, ARMONK, N.Y. and RALEIGH, N.C., June 26, 2026 — Deloitte, IBM (NYSE: IBM), and Red Hat today announced a collaboration to help protect the software supply chain against increasingly automated cyber threats. Deloitte joins the initiative as an integration collaborator for Lightwell, bringing its broader secured software supply chain architecture and cyber risk services to the large-scale enterprise open source security model deployed by IBM and Red Hat. ... Most organizations rely on a mix of first-party code, open source software, and third-party commercial software. Because a single business application can include all three, an unpatched vulnerability can introduce immediate risk across the entire corporate estate. Frontier AI models have accelerated this risk and can enable adversaries to discover and exploit zero-day flaws in minutes. Lightwell aims to help address this operational pressure by decoupling open source software security remediation from the traditional software upgrade cycle. The initiative combines an enterprise open source security model with an active engineering force. Supported by IBM and Red Hat, Lightwell coordinates upstream threat disclosures with independent maintainers while developing, testing, and backporting patches directly to the pinned software versions running in production environments. Lightwell delivers validated patches to those specific, in-use software versions, protecting critical systems without forcing disruptive upgrades. ... - Machine-Speed Remediation: Combining Red Hat and IBM’s automated patch validation with Deloitte’s orchestration services to rapidly coordinate, test, and deploy validated fixes into production repositories, limiting disruption. headline: One For The Books - Singapore Court Of Appeal Clarifies The Limits Of Auditor Liability
summary_text: In Deloitte & Touche LLP v Hin Leong Trading (Pte) Ltd [ 2026 ] SGCA 33, the Singapore Court of Appeal struck out a US $ 2.6 billion claim for trading losses brought by Hin Leong Trading (Pte) Ltd (in compulsory liquidation) ("HLT") against its former auditor, Deloitte & Touche LLP ("Deloitte") . In a landmark decision by a 5-judge coram, the Court held that even assuming HLT's pleaded case that Deloitte had negligently failed to detect the fraud and material misstatements in HLT's financial statements, the trading losses HLT sustained while insolvent were too remote to be recoverable. The Court of Appeal also took the opportunity to restate the conceptual structure of professional negligence liability - delineating the separation of duty, breach, and remoteness - and made a definitive ruling that the controversial SAAMCo principle (established in South Australia Asset Management Corporation v York Montague Ltd [ 1997 ] AC 191) does not apply in Singapore, its purpose being already served by orthodox Hadley v Baxendale remoteness rules. For claimants, the decision reinforces that a duty of care does not make a professional an insurer of the client's business. The limits of a professional's liability will very much depend on the purpose of their engagement and the responsibility assumed in that regard - the professional is not exposed to the full chain of "but for" consequences of any negligent act (even if such was proved) in the course of their engagement.

The purchase is intended to meet customer demand for new regulatory tools as Bloomberg aims to expand past traditional focus on research. ... - Bloomberg Industry Group announced the purchase of regulatory intelligence company Regology. - Regology provides customers with libraries of laws and regulatory updates tailored to their businesses, covering more than 130 countries. - The purchase is part of Bloomberg's broader strategy of expanding beyond research tools. ... Bloomberg Industry Group announced Wednesday the purchase of Palo Alto, California-based regulatory intelligence company Regology. Financial details of the transaction were not disclosed. ... Bloomberg Industry Group chief product officer Bobby Puglia told Law.com that the purchase is intended to bolster Bloomberg’s ability to meet customers’ growing demand for tools that help them navigate and comply with new regulations. ... “Organizations need better ways to monitor regular regulatory developments, to understand the impact, to respond to all the requirements,” he said. “Within Bloomberg Law, Tax and [Government] we do serve some of that, but we saw Regology as a great fit to really accelerate and fill that gap to clients.” ... Regology was founded in 2017 by a group of PwC alums to automate the process of regulatory monitoring, with an initial focus on banking and the broader financial industry. The company has roughly 70 employees, all of whom will be joining Bloomberg Industry Group as part of the transaction. Regology’s platform will continue to be offered as a standalone product and will be made available for purchase to Bloomberg Industry Group customers. ... Puglia ascribed this increased activity to the consistently growing volume and complexity of regulations companies face. headline: Singapore ministers each awarded US$177,860 in damages in Bloomberg defamation suit
summary_text: The High Court in Singapore has awarded two cabinet ministers S $ 230,000 (US $ 177,860) each in damages following a defamation trial involving financial news outlet Bloomberg and one of its reporters over the officials' property transactions. In January last year, K. Shanmugam, the coordinating minister for national security, and Tan See Leng, the manpower chief, filed separate suits against Bloomberg and its reporter Low De Wei over a story titled "Singapore mansion deals are increasingly shrouded in secrecy". The article reported that Shanmugam used a trust structure to sell a bungalow in the affluent neighbourhood of Queen Astrid Park and mentioned Tan's non-caveated purchase of a good class bungalow (GCB) in nearby Brizay Park. In a written judgment released on Tuesday, Justice Audrey Lim awarded each minister S $ 170,000 in general damages and S $ 60,000 in aggravated damages. Lim said the article conveyed to the ordinary reader that the current system lacked checks and balances and disclosure requirements where non-caveated GCB or mansion transactions were allowed to be kept secret, and that Tan and Shanmugam conducted their transactions non-transparently to take advantage of this.

The world’s largest PET producer is “working very hard” to convert its Q2 increase in spot volumes into contract arrangements to last far beyond the war-related disruptions that necessitated them, executives said during a quarterly earnings call. ... Alpek CEO Jorge Young said July 23 that although he expects continued headwinds from global overcapacity in chemicals and polymers, the company is focusing on its position as a local supplier as buyers once again re-evaluate their supply chains. ... For example, in key PET markets Alpek can – and has in 2026 – replace “some level of imports,” Young said. ... And despite revising its 2026 financial guidance sharply upward, Alpek assumes disruptions from the Iran war will subside throughout the second half of the year, narrowing reference margins and lowering ocean freight rates compared to the second quarter. ... The Mexico-headquartered company now expects significantly higher comparable EBITDA of $750 million to $850 million for 2026, versus the previous guidance of $450 million to $550 million. ... During the quarter, Alpek significantly increased spot sales, as customers sought to offset war-related disruptions to contracted volumes from other suppliers, Young said. He added that the company hopes to convert some of those spot customers into longer-term contract clients, and that the Q2 customer mix was both larger and more diverse. ... Among all Alpek’s businesses, spot business typically represents about 20% to 30% of sales, but in Q2 that share increased by about 10 percentage points, Young said. ... “We have many new names. And we have many current customers that typically buy both spot and contract,” Young said. “We have a great opportunity in front of us to retain this expanded customer base that we have with us now.” ... Existing contract customers also increased volumes, “and to an important extent there was some repricing” during the quarter, to reflect soaring prices for feedstocks – in particular crude-oil sourced paraxylene (PX) and its derivative purified terephthalic acid (PTA), which were coming from the Middle East. ... Disruption related to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz forced Alpek to turn to alternative supply, Young said, noting that volatile shipping costs for liquids brought further cost increases. ... In retrospect, while the war increased commodity pricing and spreads, Young said, for several petrochemicals and polymers, “there was probably an overreaction in March [and] April on [polymer] purchases, expanding margins and volumes significantly.” ... And while margins and volumes are yet to rebound, “we’re beginning to see some signs,” even as some Asian countries remain cautious after “learning from the lessons in April of accumulating excessive inventories,” Young said. ... Whenever inventories do begin to normalize, renewed buying “could definitely support margins” if the war-related disruptions continue. ... ### Outcome of US trade probes will address market ‘distortions’ ... Despite the uncertain future of Mexico’s longtime status as a valued US trade ally, Young expressed support for the outcome of two US Trade Representative (USTR) investigations. ... Young noted that although at the time of the call, the US had not yet announced a decision on Section 301 tariffs, Alpek expected a continuation of the underlying tariff of 10% on Mexican imports into the US. ... Later the same day, the USTR announced that 60 economies including Mexico, Canada and the EU, would be subject to a 10% tariff as of July 24. The current administration alleges that the affected countries and regions have failed to effectively prohibit the use of forced labor practices. ... Alpek also is awaiting the outcome of a second USTR investigation, looking at structural overcapacity and production in manufacturing sectors. Young said that although ultimately the investigations aim to provide fair trade conditions for producers in the US, there still is strong domestic competition in the market. ... And although he said it’s too early to forecast the impact of the latest round of tariffs, the company expects the tariffs will “address some of the distortions in the markets and bring a fair level of pricing for producers of PET and many other industries.” ... Additionally, with the US deciding against renewing the current terms of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) this month, the trade pact now shifts into an annual review process. ... However, Alpek does not expect significant headwinds, because most chemicals made in Mexico use US feedstocks “that are fully compliant with the USMCA requirements and will be fully compliant with the rules of origin. So we expect continuity from USMCA.”

summary_text: - Australia's second-largest supermarket operator heads into its result with sales momentum still building across its supermarkets and liquor arms. - Retail media and e-commerce initiatives have added a new layer to earnings growth beyond traditional grocery trading. - The result lands within a crowded final week of reporting season, alongside the country's other major supermarket group, sharpening comparisons between the two rivals. ... 1.643% Last Updated at: 2026-08-18T01:10:00Z is due to hand down its full-year result in the closing days of reporting season, arriving after a recent sales update that showed comparable supermarket sales continuing to grow at a healthy pace even as family budgets remain under pressure. ... The group's most recent trading update pointed to comparable supermarket sales growth running slightly ahead of the pace set earlier in the year, a sign that the grocery business has continued to gain traction even as broader discretionary categories elsewhere in retail have struggled. Total sales growth outpaced comparable sales growth, reflecting a continued contribution from new and refurbished store openings. ... That momentum sets a relatively high bar for the upcoming full-year result, with the market likely to focus less on whether growth continued and more on whether the pace of that growth can be sustained into the new financial year given the softer spending backdrop facing many other consumer categories. ... The group's retail media arm, which supplies advertising and data services to suppliers wanting visibility with supermarket shoppers, has become an increasingly important contributor to group earnings. This business carries a materially higher margin than traditional grocery trading, giving the group a structural lever to lift overall profitability without relying purely on food price inflation or volume growth. ... Supplier demand for this kind of targeted advertising has grown steadily as brands compete for shelf and digital visibility within the group's stores and app, and management has flagged further expansion of this segment as a priority alongside the core grocery business heading into the new financial year. ... The group's liquor ... have faced a more challenging trading environment ... business, reflecting a broader moderation trend in alcohol consumption alongside softer discretionary spending on non-essential categories. Comparable sales growth in this segment has generally lagged the supermarket division by a wide margin. ... Management has responded with a renewed focus on store network rationalisation and a sharper promotional strategy within the liquor arm, aiming to stabilise earnings in a category that continues to represent a comparatively small but still meaningful share of group revenue. ... Online grocery sales have continued to grow faster than in-store sales, prompting continued spending in automated fulfilment capability designed to serve the online channel more efficiently than manual order selection from existing store floors. This capability is central to the group's strategy for defending margin as online penetration continues to climb across the grocery category. ... The rollout of this automated capability has been a multi-period program, and progress updates alongside the full-year result will be watched closely for evidence that the spending is translating into the expected efficiency gains rather than simply adding fixed cost to the network. ... Trade-down behaviour toward private label products has remained a defining feature of grocery shopping this cycle, with families continuing to prioritise value even as headline food price inflation has eased from earlier peaks. Private label penetration has climbed steadily, supporting margin even as branded suppliers push back on shelf space and promotional terms. ... Coles and Woolworths report their full-year results within days of each other, giving the market an unusually direct opportunity to compare strategy and execution across the country's two dominant supermarket operators. Both groups have leaned into retail media and automation as growth levers beyond traditional grocery trading, though the pace and scale of execution has differed between the two. ... Coles has generally pursued a more targeted store network expansion strategy relative to its larger rival, while both groups have faced similar scrutiny over supplier relationships and pricing practices amid ongoing public and regulatory attention on supermarket competition. ... Beyond online fulfilment, the group has continued to spend on broader supply chain automation across its distribution network, aiming to lower the cost of moving product from supplier to shelf across its national store footprint. These programs typically carry significant upfront cost before delivering the expected efficiency gains over subsequent periods. ... Management commentary alongside the result will likely address the timeline for these automation programs to move from a cost centre to a clear contributor to margin expansion, a milestone the market has been awaiting for several reporting periods now. ... Wage cost growth, driven by award increases and a tight labour market for store and distribution staff, remains one of the largest cost pressures facing the group, alongside elevated energy costs across its store and distribution network. Supplier cost pass-through has partially offset these pressures, though competitive dynamics limit how much of that cost can be passed on to price-sensitive shoppers. ... Management's ability to grow earnings faster than cost inflation, rather than simply matching it, will be one of the key metrics the market scrutinises within the upcoming result, particularly given the retail media and automation initiatives are specifically designed to provide that kind of structural margin support. ... Beyond the headline profit and sales figures, attention will centre on forward commentary regarding trading conditions in the opening weeks of the new financial year, given how closely family spending patterns have tracked broader cost of living pressures across recent periods. Any signs of a further slowdown in comparable sales growth would be closely parsed against the strong momentum shown in the most recent trading update. ... Dividend continuity and capital management commentary will also be in focus, given the group's historical reputation as a reliable income-generating name within the broader consumer staples category, a reputation that has become more prized as discretionary retail names have delivered choppier results this reporting season. ... ## Supplier Relationships Under Continued Scrutiny

summary_text: # How the ACCC is using its new powers to penalise Coles ... The regulator is examining both where supermarkets open and what they charge. (Source: Supplied) ... Coles and Woolworths are facing a new level of regulatory scrutiny. Since July 1, the ACCC has gained sweeping new powers to examine Australia’s largest supermarket chains. Under the excessive grocery pricing prohibition, it can scrutinise prices, revenue, quantities sold, product margins, operating costs and supplier rebates, then dig deeper when the figures raise questions. On the very same day the law came into effect, the regulator also blocked Coles’ proposed lease of a Ka ... Coles and Woolworths are facing a new level of regulatory scrutiny. Since July 1, the ACCC has gained sweeping new powers to examine Australia’s largest supermarket chains. Under the excessive grocery pricing prohibition, it can scrutinise prices, revenue, quantities sold, product margins, operating costs and supplier rebates, then dig deeper when the figures raise questions. On the very same day the law came into effect, the regulator also blocked Coles’ proposed lease of a Kalgoorlie site for a new supermarket and Liquorland. Together, the decisions signal an ACCC increasingly willing to scrutinise supermarkets from site acquisition through to shelf pricing. The pricing prohibition applies to supermarket retailers earning more than $30 billion annually in Australia, which currently consists of the archetypal supermarket duopoly – Coles and Woolworths. A grocery price may breach the rule when it is significantly excessive compared with the cost of supplying that product plus a reasonable margin. However, there is no automatic percentage at which a price becomes unlawful. Suzanne Howari, a special counsel at Holding Redlich with a remit in Corporate and Commercial Law, says the regulator is taking “a more active role in overseeing both market structure and market conduct in the supermarket sector”. The ACCC may also consider supplier costs, freight, wages, rent and other legitimate expenses. Rises can therefore be commercially justified, but the problem begins when the retailer’s numbers struggle to explain the distance between cost and checkout. That dual interest was evident in Kalgoorlie, a small mining town of about 30,000 people, where Coles proposed a 2800-square-metre full-line supermarket and liquor store. It became the first acquisition prohibited under Australia’s new mandatory merger regime, which requires businesses to notify the ACCC of qualifying acquisitions and wait for clearance before proceeding. Upon the decision, ACCC Deputy Chair Mick Keogh noted the significance of independent supermarkets and their role as an important competitive constraint on the major supermarket chains. “They provide consumers with meaningful choice, competition on service, quality and range, and competition on price for some products.” Competition advice should be the first priorityFor Howari, the case highlights the importance of competition advice towards the beginning of the development process, besides rent, planning, construction costs and projected sales. “Ideally, before sites are secured and key commercial terms are agreed,” she said. The risk is especially pronounced in regional markets, where a single opening can divert a sizable share of household grocery spending. As Howari explained, competition law cannot be treated as a regulatory issue to be addressed shortly before completion.The ACCC’s new reach also extends to promotions; in its guidance, the regulator imagines a soft drink that regularly alternates between full price and 20 per cent off. A supermarket then doubles the full price and advertises a 30 per cent discount, which leaves customers paying far more than before. The watchdog can examine the entire pricing history, including supplier rebates, allowances and promotional funding behind the “sale”. It may also compare prices across regions and investigate whether higher charges in areas with fewer competitors genuinely reflect greater supply costs. Coles and Woolworths must retain relevant pricing information for at least three years, while false or misleading responses to compulsory information requests can create further legal trouble. The modern supermarket may still live by the weekly special, but the ACCC now wants to see how it works.Regulatory scrutiny can begin with the land, continue through the lease and follow a product all the way to the checkout basket. Developers may require a competitive analysis before securing an anchor tenant, and subsequently, pricing teams will need records that stand the test of time. As Howari explains, businesses that can be proactive by identifying and managing competition risks early will be far better positioned to avoid lengthy investigations. “Strengthen governance, competition law compliance and internal risk assessment processes, particularly in areas that have become ACCC enforcement priorities,” she said. summary_text: Australian supermarket chains Coles and Woolworths have carried out early-stage trials of facial recognition technology to explore options for tackling rising crime and violent incidents in stores. According to the Australian Financial Review, the trials are part of a broader retail sector push to assess the technology for staff protection, particularly in Victoria, where major chains have recorded growing levels of theft and other offences. Both companies have already put millions of dollars into anti-theft measures such as exit gates, cameras covering bagging areas, and body-worn cameras for staff. headline: ACCC probes Aldi, Coles after Four Corners tomato-sourcing claims
summary_text: The country's consumer watchdog has initiated inquiries into Aldi, Coles and Leggo's after a Four Corners investigation by ABC News raised allegations that tomato products that are advertised as Australia-grown were actually sourced from China. The report came from a series of tests by forensic laboratory Source Certain, which examined 221 processed tomato brands over several months and found 22 per cent of them were not from the claimed country of origin. The businesses in question told Inside Retail that they reject the claims raised by Four Corners. At the same time, they all committed to reviewing their own supply chains, with Coles promising to commission independent testing. Simplot, the widely-accused maker of Leggo's tomato products, went on to challenge the testing methodology and criticise its lack of transparency.

The testing was commissioned by the ABC's Four Corners and conducted by forensic laboratory Source Certain, which the broadcaster said has worked with the US Federal Bureau of Investigation, Scotland Yard, Interpol and the Australian Federal Police. The findings could further erode consumers' trust in Australia's supermarket sector, which is already under scrutiny after pricing controversies.

headline: Enterprises are overpaying for simple AI queries — Snowflake's gateway now auto-routes to cut costs up to 3x | VentureBeat
summary_text: Enterprises are overpaying for simple AI queries — Snowflake's gateway now auto-routes to cut costs up to 3x | VentureBeat ... Snowflake’s Cortex AI Gateway now offers dynamic model routing to address that: enterprises can select “auto” instead of a fixed model, and the system routes each task to whichever model offers the best combination of quality and cost. Snowflake said the capability can cut token costs by as much as 3x on some workloads — a figure from the company’s own internal testing — after finding that simple questions were often handled by its most capable model, making responses more expensive and slower than necessary. ... The move lands amid a broader industry shift toward automated model routing. Databricks, AWS, Google Cloud and Nvidia have all announced some form of model routing technology. Snowflake argues that model routing is more complex than just price and performance, it's also about governance and context. ... The capability builds on Cortex AI Gateway, which Snowflake launched in July 2026 as a governance layer for agent and model traffic. Before dynamic routing, model selection ran off a static list per task rather than a true fallback system, Gultekin said. ... Snowflake's recent acquisition of Natoma adds another layer. The deal brings more than 100 MCP connectors with scoped, governed access. An agent could get read-only access to a connected tool like email, for example, rather than broader permissions. ... Snowflake recently announced its Horizon Context and Cortex Sense tools that provide context capabilities. ... There is no shortage of technologies in the model routing space. OpenRouter is one of the most widely known options, providing a platform that enables organizations to route based on cost and performance. Nvidia on August 11 announced Switchyard as a technology layer to help route AI model choice. Databricks has an offering as well with Smart Routing for its Unity AI Gateway. "The interesting part is what it says about where differentiation has moved," Sanjeev Mohan, Principal and Founder, SanjMo, told VentureBeat. "Snowflake isn't really selling routing, it's selling routing that never leaves the governed data boundary, with access controls, tagging, and cost attribution already attached." ... Mohan added that for a company whose data and compliance already center on Snowflake, routing that keeps data in place and attributes spend by team is a real lever on that problem. For a company without that center of gravity, a neutral gateway may route across more models with less friction. ... Mohan frames the market as three distinct camps rather than one competitive field. Databricks approaches governance from data engineering and ML lineage. Its Unity Catalog governs data, models and pipelines for teams building and training models. Snowflake approaches governance from analytics and access control, governing who can touch which data and attributing usage across business units. A third camp includes neutral gateways such as OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Portkey and hyperscaler routers like Azure AI Foundry. These compete on model breadth and avoiding lock-in rather than deep governance. ... The right starting point depends on where an enterprise's data already lives. A Snowflake shop gets more value from in-platform routing that respects its existing access model and bills back to cost centers than from raw model breadth, according to Mohan. A Databricks-centric team worried about lineage across training and deployment is better served by a gateway built around that same lineage. A multi-platform or model-first team that wants maximum choice with minimal lock-in fits better with a neutral gateway, the same pitch behind OpenRouter's valuation.

Snowflake has shipped plenty of features for running code inside its warehouses, but until now it left the deployment of the warehouse objects themselves to third-party tools. That changes with Snowflake DCM Projects, which reached general availability on August 7, 2026. DCM, short for Database Change Management, lets you define databases, tables, tasks, and other Snowflake objects declaratively in SQL files, then let Snowflake figure out the diff and apply the changes. The headline: you can now version-control and idempotently deploy your Snowflake infrastructure without an external state file or a separate Terraform runner. ... The move matters because every team running Snowflake at scale already has a deployment problem. Some use Terraform or dbt, some run hand-rolled SQL scripts in GitHub Actions, and most have a tangled mix of both. DCM Projects is Snowflake's native answer: a declarative layer that handles the plan, the diff, and the apply, all inside the account. For teams that already think about pipeline architecture choices, this adds a new dimension to the build question. ... One important nuance: the explicit PREVIEW and TEST commands are still in Preview as of the GA release. The GA plan-then-deploy story relies on EXECUTE DCM PROJECT, which applies changes. If you want a dedicated dry-run verb before applying, that specific SQL command is not yet production-ready. Plan accordingly: test in a lower environment where EXECUTE is safe, and treat staging as your dry run until the PREVIEW command ships as GA. ... Most teams deploying Snowflake objects today use one of two approaches. Terraform with the Snowflake provider gives you declarative state and a plan output, but it runs outside Snowflake and requires a state file you have to manage. Raw SQL scripts in CI/CD give you full control but no diff, no drift detection, and no idempotency without careful scripting. DCM Projects splits the difference. ... The trade-off is clear. DCM Projects removes the need for an external runner and a state file, which simplifies CI/CD and cuts the number of moving parts. But it locks your deployment definitions to Snowflake. If your infrastructure spans AWS, dbt, and Snowflake, Terraform still has a role for the parts outside Snowflake. If Snowflake is your whole world, DCM is the simpler path. ... Here is the good news for anyone who owns the Snowflake bill: DCM Projects does not introduce a separate credit charge. The feature runs within your existing Snowflake account. The compute used for planning and applying changes runs on a warehouse, so the cost is the warehouse compute you are already paying for. There is no per-execution fee, no marketplace listing, and no premium edition requirement called out in the GA announcement. ... Source: Snowflake release notes. ... The chart above shows the capability split at GA. 7 capabilities are generally available, including the DEFINE statement core, Jinja templating, and the plan-then-deploy workflow. 8 capabilities remain in Preview, and several of them are the governance and pipeline objects you most need for production. ... The GA is real, but it is not complete. These capabilities remain in Preview: ... - TEST and PREVIEW commands: the dry-run verbs are not GA yet - GitHub Actions for DCM Projects: no native CI integration yet - DEFINE PIPE: cannot declaratively manage Snowpipe objects - DEFINE STREAM: cannot declaratively manage streams - DEFINE MASKING POLICY: cannot declaratively manage masking policies - DEFINE ROW ACCESS POLICY: cannot declaratively manage row access policies - ATTACH TAG: cannot declaratively attach tags to objects - Inherited grants and container-level MANAGE GRANTS: advanced grant patterns not supported ... If your governance story depends on masking policies, row access policies, or tag-based protections, DCM Projects cannot manage those objects declaratively today. You will still need imperative SQL or Terraform for that layer. For a deeper look at those governance objects, see our guide on Snowflake RBAC and masking. ... Similarly, if your pipeline uses streams, you are out of luck for declarative management. You can declaratively define dynamic tables and tasks, but streams remain imperative. For teams building event-driven pipelines, this is the gap to watch. ... Start with objects that are fully GA: databases, tables, tasks, and dynamic tables. These cover the bulk of what most teams deploy repeatedly. Leave pipes, streams, and governance policies in your existing tooling for now. ... DCM Projects GA is a genuine step forward for Snowflake-native DevOps. It removes the external state file and the separate IaC runner for the objects it covers, and it does so without a new line item on your bill. The gaps are real but bounded: governance objects and streams will come, and until they do, you run a hybrid stack. If you are starting a new Snowflake project today, begin with DCM definitions. If you are running a mature Terraform setup, do not rip it out, but start migrating the object types DCM supports and shrink your Terraform footprint over time.

TORU YAMANAKA/AFP via Getty Images China's Haier is expanding in Japan's appliance market, where it says it overtook Panasonic to reach second place in washing machines last year — a shift that, as reported by ETNews, has some Korean industry watchers warning their own companies could be next if they treat low-margin "white goods" as expendable. ... The story is less about cheap imports than about a patient strategy walking through a door Japanese makers chose to leave open. As Japan's electronics giants stepped back from low-margin home appliances to concentrate on higher-value businesses, Haier moved into the vacant space — and it did so with a playbook worth understanding on its own terms. ... In its fiscal 2025 annual report, Haier said the combined share of its own brand and AQUA reached 17.7% of Japan's washing-machine market, good for second place. That figure is Haier's own, drawn from its annual report; independent import data points the same direction, with Chinese-made washers accounting for the overwhelming majority of Japan's washing-machine imports. Haier also says its combined Haier-plus-AQUA share ranks first in Japan's refrigeration category, and it touts a leading combined position across refrigerators, freezers, and washers. Panasonic, for its part, had already slipped from first place in washers to second in 2023, before Haier's claimed overtaking. ... The strategy pairs a premium AQUA line — trading on Sanyo's half-century of washer engineering and the trust Japanese buyers still place in the name — with Haier's own mid-to-low-priced brand beneath it. That lets one company occupy both the premium and budget shelves under names local consumers already accept, rather than fighting uphill as a foreign newcomer. It is the same localization playbook Haier used in the U.S. by buying GE Appliances in 2016 and keeping the American name. Framed plainly, this is a legitimate competitive achievement: smart acquisitions, local brand-building, and pricing discipline, not a mystery. ... Haier's advance owes much to Japanese makers retreating from white goods — and that retreat was a choice, not a defeat. Hitachi, long a washing-machine leader, has weighed selling its home-appliance business since last year and spun off its consumer-electronics arm in April, with its parent focusing on air conditioning. Across the Japanese electronics industry, the pattern has been an active contraction: stepping back from low-margin, fiercely competitive downstream products to concentrate capital on higher-value components and businesses. Exiting a commodity-hardware category where you compete mainly on price can be a perfectly rational decision. ... The deeper debate the Japanese case has stirred among Korean industry voices is about what a low-margin appliance is actually worth. Their argument: a refrigerator, washer, or air conditioner is not just a one-time hardware sale but a physical node that sits in a home for a decade, and increasingly a connected one — a consumer touchpoint and installed base underpinning smart-home platforms, service networks, and component supply chains. On this view, ceding the "boring" box today could undercut tomorrow's higher-margin AI-appliance, subscription, and home-energy businesses, because those are built on the foothold the hardware provides. "The changes in Japan's appliance market are a case study in what happens the moment you lose the manufacturing touchpoint," one industry insider said. ... That is a strategic argument, and a contested one. The counter-consideration is the very logic behind the Japanese exits: if a hardware category is genuinely unprofitable, defending it for the sake of a future platform may cost more than it returns, and focusing on components or services can be the sounder bet. Notably, Korean firms are not standing still either — LG has moved to re-enter Japan's premium appliance market after a roughly 12-year absence, with AI-equipped washers, suggesting the "touchpoint" thesis is one some are choosing to act on. ... Japanese electronics companies have increasingly stepped back from low-margin "white goods" like washers and refrigerators to focus on higher-value businesses, a trend rooted in decades of price competition, higher domestic costs, and the loss of cost advantage in commodity hardware and display panels. headline: Flint Group to showcase inks, coatings, and digital print solutions at LOUPE Americas -
summary_text: Packaging converters and label printers can explore Flint Group Packaging Solutions’ latest label and packaging technologies at LOUPE Americas 2026, taking place from 15-17 September in Chicago. At Booth 5821, Flint Group Packaging Solutions will showcase its largest-ever event portfolio, featuring ink, coating, and digital print technologies from its Narrow Web and Flint Group Digital Xeikon business segments, including EkoCure® Dual Cure inks for conventional UV and UV LED printing. ... Also on display will be Flexocure® LEAP, the company’s latest UV conventional ink innovation. Built on a new resin platform, Flexocure LEAP helps reduce the risk of photoinitiator migration while supporting packaging integrity and future regulatory compliance. The company’s Narrow Web business segment will also highlight its Hydrokett and Hydrofilm water-based ink systems for narrow web paper and film applications, as well as its broad portfolio of conventional and digital coatings designed to enhance both functional performance and visual appeal. Flint Group Digital Xeikon will run live demonstrations of three engines on the stand: ... - TX500: Powered by TITON dry toner technology, the TX500 delivers food-safe, durable label production without the need for additional varnish or lamination steps. - PX3300 HD: Built on a 1200 dpi UV inkjet platform with PantherCure UV inks, this engine covers the highest color gamut at speeds of 70 m/min in CMYK+W. - Ecolyne: A subscription-based digital label press, designed to give commercial printers and converters a low-risk, fully managed entry into the label market. In addition, Flint Group Digital Xeikon experts will be available to discuss the IDERA solution for corrugated post-print. IDERA is the company’s single-pass UV inkjet platform purpose-built for high-quality, high-speed digital printing on corrugated board. Visitors can request printed samples and learn how IDERA supports one of the fastest-growing segments in digital packaging. Ser van de Graaf, sales & marketing director for Flint Group Digital Xeikon North America, said: “Converters need technologies that align with their production requirements, and we are thrilled to run live demonstrations of our digital innovations throughout the show. Our digital portfolio includes dry toner and UV inkjet solutions to support a wide range of applications, volumes, and substrates, from entry-level production through to high-volume label printing. With TITON technology, we also offer a unique combination of dry toner print quality and UV inkjet durability.” ... At LOUPE, the company will also demonstrate FlintLink, Flint Group Packaging Solutions’ secure customer portal providing 24/7 access to SDS and other business documentation, order management, troubleshooting, and remote technical support. Visitors can also learn about the latest developments in VIVO Color Solutions, a cutting-edge, end-to-end digital color management platform designed to help printers achieve fast, accurate color matching across the pressroom. By enabling precise brand color reproduction and incorporating press return functionality to simplify ink reuse, VIVO supports smarter workflows, improves operational efficiency, and helps reduce ink inventory costs. Kenneth Keathley, director of Narrow Web North America, concluded: “We are excited to bring the full strength of Flint Group Packaging Solutions to LOUPE Americas 2026. Our UV, UV LED, water-based, and coating technologies are designed to integrate seamlessly into existing operations, providing stable performance, predictable curing, and support for evolving regulatory compliance requirements. This event is all about connecting with customers, understanding their goals, and helping them identify practical ways to improve their operations. We invite attendees to visit Booth 5821 and discover how Flint Group Packaging Solutions can help support their business today and into the future.”

headline: Flint Group Packaging Solutions prepares for LOUPE Americas - Label and Narrow Web
summary_text: # Flint Group Packaging Solutions prepares for LOUPE Americas ... L&NW speaks to Anna Niewiadomska and Paulo Vieira about the company's plans for LOUPE Americas and how its meeting market demand. ... Flint Group Packaging Solutions will bring a new identity to the similarly refreshed LOUPE Americas. To learn more about the company’s latest products, L&NW sat down with Anna Niewiadomska, Marketing Manager, Narrow Web, and Paulo Vieira, Global Key Accounts Technical Director & Packaging Coatings Director. ... L&NW: What are your expectations for LOUPE and the new format?AN: The new LOUPE format is exciting and represents a natural progression for the event, building on its proven past success while delivering additional value for visitors. We see it as a great fit for Flint Group Packaging Solutions as a business, as we already operate across labels, flexible packaging, and paper & board. The broader scope simply reflects the reality of many of our customers’ businesses today. Converters and brand owners are seeking new ways to optimize performance and sustainability across their entire portfolio. The expanded LOUPE creates a more relevant environment for holding those conversations and demonstrating how integrated solutions can support them moving forward. For us, LOUPE remains a key platform to engage with customers and partners across North America. It provides an opportunity to show how Flint Group Packaging Solutions supports the industry as a solutions partner rather than solely a supplier – delivering inks, coatings, and digital print technologies alongside value-added programs that improve efficiency, reduce waste, and support regulatory and sustainability goals. The event fosters meaningful discussions on collaboration and innovation. ... L&NW: What products will the company highlight at its LOUPE booth?AN: Our primary focus will always be on inks. Our focus is to present Flint Group Packaging Solutions as an integrated supplier of inks, coatings and digital print solutions. ... As it pertains to inks, the solutions we deliver are integral to achieving high-quality, safe, and more sustainable printing. At LOUPE, we plan to showcase our UV LED technologies across the EkoCure range, alongside our water-based ink systems. Both ranges are designed to help printers improve energy efficiency and reduce their environmental impact while maintaining consistent print quality. We will also highlight our Flexocure LEAP ink series – a food contact material solution for the US market – which helps to simplify regulatory compliance and testing. ... Alongside these inks, we will highlight a selection of our coatings for converters seeking to enhance print with added functionality, protection, or visual impact. Our teams will be ready to discuss technologies that support recyclability and circular packaging goals, such as our Evolution coatings and primers. Our intention is to show how our inks and coatings work together as a complete system for achieving quality, efficiency, and sustainability – rather than as standalone products. ... Rounding out our integrated approach, we will also highlight our Flint Group Digital Xeikon business and digital consumables. Visitors can see demonstrations of three engines running live digital print jobs. ... L&NW: What trends are you seeing with coatings?PV: One of the main shifts we have seen in relation to coatings is the move away from viewing them as a purely decorative finishing step. Increasingly, coatings are recognized as a core strategic component within the overall packaging design and performance architecture, and are considered earlier in the overall development process as converters recognize the influence they can have across everything from recyclability to durability and brand perception. ... Sustainability remains a major driver of this shift. Coatings can play an important role in enabling recyclability by facilitating de-inking and supporting mono-material structures that are simpler to reprocess into new material. They also support the growing demand for functional performance by providing barrier properties, surface protection, and the overall preservation of graphic integrity throughout the value chain. ... L&NW: What are the benefits of your newest coating products?PV: Our coating technologies help converters combine strong visual impact with lasting functional performance. For example, our DecaCode portfolio elevates packaging designs without making them more complex than necessary, avoiding the need for additional laminates or secondary materials. Products can be selected to deliver a range of desired finishes while providing the durability needed to maintain a premium look and feel throughout distribution and handling. ... Consistency is another key benefit as our coatings help preserve color integrity and surface quality from production through to the point of sale or delivery, which is increasingly important in e-commerce-driven supply chains. They also give designers greater creative freedom, enabling distinctive textures and finishes that help products stand out. Importantly, this is delivered with reliable performance across different substrates and print technologies, alongside shorter, more flexible production runs. ... We will also highlight our Evolution range, which includes a caustic-resistant overprint varnish for floatable materials and a de-inking primer for crystallizable PET shrink sleeves. These products simplify recycling and enable greater quantities of material to be reclaimed, thus aligning packaging performance with circular economy requirements.

headline: Flint Global Expansion Boosts Europe Presence – Brusselsmirror
summary_text: Flint Global Expansion Boosts Europe Presence ... Consulting firm Flint Global has expanded its presence in Western Europe by integrating the public affairs practice of Considerati. The move adds a team of about 20 professionals based in Amsterdam and Brussels, strengthening Flint Global’s advisory capabilities across the Benelux region. ... The transaction marks another step in Flint Global’s international growth strategy as demand continues to rise for political, regulatory, and public affairs advice across Europe. The newly added team will become part of Flint Global’s operations while continuing to support clients in the Netherlands, Belgium, and the wider European market. ... Founded in 2015, Flint Global provides political and regulatory consulting services to businesses, investors, and organizations operating in complex policy environments. The firm advises clients on government relations, competition policy, regulation, and political developments that may affect business operations. ... The company currently operates offices in London, Brussels, Paris, Berlin, Amsterdam, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Melbourne. Its international network allows clients to receive support across multiple jurisdictions while responding to changing regulatory and political conditions. ... Thomas Barros-Tastets, Managing Partner for Europe at Flint Global, welcomed the expansion and praised Considerati’s public affairs team. ... He said the two firms share similar values and long-term ambitions. According to Barros-Tastets, combining local expertise with an international platform will allow the firm to better serve clients across different markets and strengthen its presence throughout Europe. ... Founder and Chief Executive Officer Ton Wagemans said the public affairs team has built a strong reputation under the leadership of Bart Pegge. He also highlighted the growth of the firm’s Brussels office, particularly in advising clients in the technology and healthcare sectors. ... The expansion reflects increasing demand for specialist advice in areas where government policy, regulation, and business strategy intersect. Companies operating across Europe are facing evolving rules on technology, competition, sustainability, healthcare, and digital markets, increasing the need for experienced public affairs advisers. ... As part of the transaction, Bart Pegge will join Flint Global as a partner and become a member of the firm’s leadership team. He said the move provides new opportunities for both clients and employees by combining local knowledge with a wider international advisory network. ... Pegge added that Flint Global shares Considerati’s commitment to client service and long-term growth. He believes the combined business will allow clients to benefit from broader expertise across European markets while maintaining strong local support. ... Industry analysts note that consolidation among consulting firms has increased in recent years as clients seek integrated advice covering public policy, regulatory compliance, legal issues, and government relations. Expanding geographic reach has also become an important competitive advantage for firms serving multinational businesses. ... The addition of Considerati’s public affairs practice is expected to strengthen Flint Global’s position in the Netherlands and Belgium while enhancing its ability to advise clients on European Union policy and regulatory developments from its expanded Brussels and Amsterdam teams. ... With the new team now joining the organization, Flint Global plans to continue growing its advisory services across Europe. The company says the expanded platform will help clients navigate increasingly complex political and regulatory environments while supporting long-term business and investment decisions across international markets.

headline: KDV Label Opens New Waukesha Manufacturing Plant
summary_text: KDV Label has opened the doors on a sprawling new 117,000-square-foot manufacturing facility near Les Paul Parkway in Waukesha, consolidating what had been scattered local operations under a single roof built with room to grow even bigger down the line. The custom label manufacturer marked the occasion with a grand-opening event on August 5, welcoming customers, business partners, suppliers, and community members to tour the new building and watch live demonstrations of its label-printing capabilities. ... The facility sits at 2230 Corporate Drive and was designed and built by Brookfield-based Briohn Building Corporation, which broke ground on the site in May 2025, according to KDV Label. As reported by Greater Milwaukee Today, KDV Label President and CEO Keith Walz noted the company broke ground on the site roughly a year before opening it, and that the new plant includes manufacturing space, printing presses, offices, and warehousing all in one location. The site was engineered with room for a future 39,000-square-foot addition, giving the company a clear runway for further expansion. ... KDV Label expects that bringing its Waukesha operations together under one roof will make it easier for teams to collaborate and improve the flow of materials and work through the plant, per the same account. The company manufactures custom labels for the food, beverage, personal care, dairy, automotive, and specialty consumer goods industries, and the new operation is built to support pressure-sensitive and digital labels, expanded content labels, unsupported film labels, variable data labels, and promotional labels. Walz said the facility reflects the company's commitment and positions it to keep delivering service, quality, and partnership to customers, according to a company news release cited by Greater Milwaukee Today. ... The expanded facility provides additional production capacity at a moment when demand for custom labels is increasing, the outlet reports. KDV Label said the investment will help the company respond to that growing customer demand while preserving the quality and attention to detail associated with its products. The expansion also includes investment in label-printing technology, workforce development, and relationships with customers and suppliers. ... The grand-opening event featured demonstrations of technology supporting KDV's continued growth, and a photograph provided by the City of Waukesha shows Walz holding scissors alongside Waukesha Mayor Alicia Halvensleben at the ribbon-cutting. KDV Label was founded in 1974 by Karen and Dick Vaughn in a family garage and was later expanded four-fold under second-generation leader Shane Vaughn, who served as CEO for 27 years before retiring in April 2023. Keith Walz took over as president and CEO that same month after serving as chief financial officer since 2021, bringing prior executive experience from Brady Corporation and Osborn LLC. ... Milwaukee-based private equity firm Mason Wells acquired KDV Label and sister entity I-Graphics LLC in June 2021 in partnership with members of the Vaughn family and company management, according to Mason Wells. Beyond its Waukesha headquarters, KDV Label operates manufacturing locations in Sugar Grove, Illinois, and Loveland, Colorado, the latter formerly run as I-Graphics LLC. The company expanded its Midwestern footprint further in July 2023 by acquiring Selective Label & Printing, Inc., a custom label printer in Sugar Grove that brought complementary flexographic and digital printing operations. ... KDV Label's operational track record has also drawn industry recognition: the company won the Tag and Label Manufacturers Institute Eugene Singer Award for Management Excellence in the medium-sized converter category in both 2024 and 2025, an award that evaluates ratio studies measuring growth and cost management. Total capital expenditures for the Waukesha buildout and any net change in the company's overall headcount were not disclosed in available materials. ... KDV Label's new plant lands amid a wider wave of industrial investment across Waukesha County. Hoodline previously reported that The Gund Company proposed a 110,000-square-foot Philip Drive expansion in June, part of a sustained run of demand for industrial space in the area that has also included major local capital projects, such as Carroll University's recently opened business and technology building.

headline: CHEP Owner Brambles Lifts Annual Profit 4% Despite Repair Constraints -- Update | MarketScreener Hong Kong
summary_text: # CHEP Owner Brambles Lifts Annual Profit 4% Despite Repair Constraints -- Update Published on 08/20/2026 at 05:56 am HKT ... -3.44% By Stuart Condie SYDNEY--Global pallet supplier Brambles reported a 4% rise in annual profit, meeting its downgraded guidance despite a larger-than-expected financial hit from the U.S. repair constraints that prompted a historic selloff of its stock. Australia-listed Brambles, which leases out pallets under the CHEP brand, on Thursday reported an annual underlying profit of $1.49 billion, up by 4% on the prior year once currency moves were stripped out. Sales revenue for the 12 months through June rose by 2% to $7.04 billion, also on a constant-currency basis. Brambles had initially guided for an 8% to 11% rise in underlying profit, but slashed its outlook in May to between 3% and 5% on an increase in costs from unexpected capacity constraints at subcontracted pallet service centers in parts of the U.S. The downgrade prompted the stock's largest one-day drop since 2002. Several formerly bullish analysts cut their rating and the consensus forecast for annual underlying profit fell from $1.565 billion to $1.48 billion ahead of Thursday's result announcement. Analysts had been looking for sales of $7.04 billion, according to data compiled by Visible Alpha. Brambles said its underlying profit had taken a $90 million hit from the U.S. repair constraints, exceeding its prior estimate by 50%. The effect included lost revenue and additional transport and plant costs, it said. More positively, additional fourth-quarter pallet purchases to address shortages cost $40 million, $20 million less than expected, as it utilized excess pallets in storage. Brambles, which raised its dividend to $0.2315 from $0.2083, said it expected to resolve the constraint issues by the end of December, as previously flagged. "Our actions are already delivering positive results, with customer order fulfilment improving materially since mid April," Chief Executive Graham Chipchase said. "We remain on track to resolve the repair capacity constraints by the end of the first half of FY27 and position our U.S. business to strengthen customer relationships and pursue growth." Payment for the new pallets is due in the December half and Brambles expects to spend another $60 million on an additional 2 million new pallets in the same period, resulting in a total cash outflow of $100 million. Brambles expects fiscal 2027 free cash flow before dividends of between $800 million and $950 million, down from $1.05 billion in the fiscal year just ended. It expects underlying profit growth of between 2% and 6%, and sales revenue growth of between 2% and 4%, both in constant currency terms. Brambles didn't add to the $400 million buyback extension announced in May. It expects to complete the current on-market buyback in the current fiscal year.
